q: Which postulate of the kinetic molecular theory explains why a gas spreads out to fill any container it is placed in?
o: Its molecules are attracted strongly to the walls of the container
Its molecules lose energy every time they collide
Its molecules are packed closely together in fixed positions
Its molecules move continuously and randomly in all directions
x: Because gas molecules are in constant random motion in every direction, they spread through the whole space available. Gas molecules are far apart, not packed, and their collisions are elastic.

q: The kinetic molecular theory assumes there are no forces between gas molecules except during collisions. So, between two collisions, the speed of a molecule:
x: With no force acting on it between collisions, a molecule moves in a straight line at constant speed. Its speed changes only when it collides with another molecule or a wall.

q: Two flasks at the same temperature contain 1 mol of helium and 2 mol of neon. Compared with the helium, the total kinetic energy of the neon molecules is:
x: Average kinetic energy per molecule depends only on temperature, so it is the same for both gases. Neon has twice as many molecules, so its total kinetic energy is twice as large; molar mass does not matter.

q: A gas exerts the same pressure on every wall of its container. According to the kinetic molecular theory, this is because:
o: Molecules move faster towards the top of the container
Molecules attract each wall with the same force
The heavier molecules always settle at the bottom
Molecular motion is random, so on average every part of the wall is struck equally often
x: Random motion means no direction is preferred, so each area of wall receives the same number of impacts per second on average. Gravity has a negligible effect on a gas in a small container.

q: The kinetic molecular theory assumes that, within one pure gas sample, every molecule has:
o: The same speed as every other molecule at a given temperature
The same mass and size as every other molecule
A mass that depends on how fast it moves
x: The theory assumes that all molecules of a given gas are identical in mass and size. Their speeds vary from molecule to molecule; only the average kinetic energy is fixed by temperature.

q: Two gases are in identical flasks at the same pressure, each containing the same number of molecules. From PV = ⅓mNc̄², the gas with heavier molecules must have:
o: Molecules that do not collide with the walls
x: With P, V and N the same, the product mc̄² must be the same for both gases. A larger mass m therefore needs a smaller c̄²: heavier molecules move more slowly.

q: More gas is pumped into a rigid container at constant temperature, and the pressure rises. According to the kinetic molecular theory, this is because:
o: More molecules strike the walls every second
Each collision with the wall is now more forceful
The molecules now attract one another more strongly
x: At constant temperature the average speed, and so the force of each impact, is unchanged. More molecules in the same space means more impacts per second, so the pressure rises.

q: A gas is heated from 27 °C to 327 °C. The average kinetic energy of its molecules:
x: Average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature: 27 °C = 300 K and 327 °C = 600 K, so it doubles. The 12-fold answer comes from wrongly using Celsius temperatures.

q: The motion in which gas molecules move as a whole from one place to another is called:
x: Translational motion carries a molecule from one place to another, and it is the motion responsible for gas pressure and diffusion. Vibration and rotation do not move the molecule through space.

q: Smoke particles in still air, seen under a microscope, move about in an irregular zig-zag way. This observation shows that:
o: They are being hit unevenly by fast-moving air molecules
The smoke particles are attracted to one another
Air molecules are at rest and the particles push them
The smoke particles are themselves gas molecules
x: This Brownian motion is caused by unequal bombardment of the particles by invisible air molecules that are moving rapidly and randomly. It is direct evidence for the motion of gas molecules.

q: The pressure of a gas is increased at constant temperature. The mean free path of its molecules:
o: Increases, because the molecules move faster
Stays the same, because the temperature is constant
Increases, because there are fewer collisions
Decreases, because the molecules are closer together
x: Higher pressure at constant temperature packs the molecules closer, so a molecule travels a shorter distance before its next collision. The average speed is unchanged because the temperature is unchanged.

q: Hydrogen (M = 2) is at 300 K. At what temperature would oxygen (M = 32) have the same root mean square speed? (Use speed = √(3RT/M).)
x: Equal speeds need equal T/M: 300/2 = T/32, so T = 300 × 16 = 4800 K. Using √16 = 4 gives the wrong value 1200 K.

q: At 25 °C, the molecules of which gas have the lowest average speed? (H 1, He 4, C 12, N 14, Cl 35.5)
x: At the same temperature all molecules have the same average kinetic energy, so the heaviest molecules move slowest. Cl₂ (M = 71) is the heaviest here.

q: A gas in a sealed rigid container is cooled. Which of the following does NOT decrease?
o: The average speed of the molecules
The number of collisions with the walls per second
The number of molecules in the container
x: The container is sealed, so the number of molecules stays the same. Cooling slows the molecules, so they hit the walls less often and less hard, and the pressure falls.

q: Molecules in a gas have a spread of speeds. When the temperature is raised, the fraction of molecules moving at high speeds:
o: Increases, and the average speed also increases
Decreases, while the average speed increases
Stays the same, while the average speed increases
Increases, but the average speed stays the same
x: Heating shifts the whole speed distribution towards higher values: more molecules move fast and the average speed rises. Some molecules still move slowly, but fewer than before.

q: Which pair of conditions is NOT the same as STP?
x: STP is 0 °C (273 K) and 1 atm (760 mm Hg or 101325 Pa). 25 °C is room temperature, not standard temperature.

q: How many molecules are present in 5.6 dm³ of any ideal gas at STP? (Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
x: Moles = 5.6/22.4 = 0.25 mol; molecules = 0.25 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.505 × 10²³. The 2.408 × 10²⁴ value comes from multiplying by 4 instead of dividing.

q: A mixture of 0.5 mol of O₂ and 0.5 mol of N₂ behaves ideally. What volume does it occupy at STP?
x: Volume at STP depends only on the total number of moles: 0.5 + 0.5 = 1 mol, which occupies 22.4 dm³. The kind of gas does not matter.

q: What is the mass of 2.24 dm³ of sulphur dioxide, SO₂, at STP? (S = 32, O = 16)
x: 2.24 dm³ at STP is 0.1 mol; M(SO₂) = 32 + 32 = 64 g mol⁻¹, so mass = 0.1 × 64 = 6.4 g.

q: A gas has a density of 1.25 g dm⁻³ at STP. Its molar mass is about:
x: Molar mass = density × molar volume = 1.25 × 22.4 = 28 g mol⁻¹. Dividing 22.4 by 1.25 instead gives the wrong 17.9.

q: At STP, which sample has the largest volume? (H 1, He 4, O 16, Cl 35.5)
x: 4 g of H₂ is 2 mol, which occupies 44.8 dm³. Each of the other samples is 1 mol, which occupies 22.4 dm³.

q: Volumes of gases are usually compared at STP because:
o: All gases have the same mass at STP
Gases do not expand or contract at STP
Gases behave as liquids at STP
The volume of a gas depends on its temperature and pressure, so fixed reference conditions are needed
x: A gas volume changes with both temperature and pressure, so it is only meaningful to compare volumes under agreed standard conditions. Gases still expand and contract at STP.

q: A gas occupies 3 dm³ at 760 mm Hg. At constant temperature, it is compressed until the pressure is 1140 mm Hg. Its new volume is:
x: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂: V₂ = 760 × 3/1140 = 2 dm³. The 4.5 dm³ value comes from inverting the pressure ratio.

q: The volume of a fixed mass of gas is halved at constant temperature. The number of collisions per second on each unit area of the wall:
o: Stays the same, so the pressure stays the same
Doubles, but the pressure stays the same
x: The same molecules at the same speed in half the volume are twice as crowded, so they strike each area of wall twice as often. This doubles the pressure, as Boyle's law predicts.

q: A sample of gas has a volume of 12 dm³ at 1 atm. At the same temperature, which pair of pressure and volume could also belong to this sample?
x: At constant temperature PV stays at 1 × 12 = 12 dm³ atm. Only 3 atm × 4 dm³ gives 12; the others give 108, 20 and 16.

q: A gas bubble rises from the bottom of a lake, where the pressure is 3 atm, to the surface, where it is 1 atm. If the temperature stays the same, its volume:
x: By Boyle's law, volume is inversely proportional to pressure. The pressure falls to one-third, so the volume becomes three times larger.

q: Graphs of volume against pressure are drawn for the same gas sample at two temperatures, T₁ and T₂, where T₂ is higher than T₁. Compared with the T₁ curve, the T₂ curve:
o: Lies further from the axes, giving a larger volume at each pressure
Lies closer to the axes, giving a smaller volume at each pressure
Is a straight line instead of a curve
x: Each isotherm obeys PV = constant, and the constant is larger at the higher temperature. So at any pressure the volume is larger, and the T₂ curve lies further from the axes.

q: Boyle's law holds only when:
o: The pressure and the temperature of the gas are kept constant
The volume and the mass of the gas are kept constant
The mass and the temperature of the gas are kept constant
The pressure and the volume of the gas are kept constant
x: Boyle's law relates pressure and volume, so both of these change, while the amount (mass) of gas and its temperature are fixed.

q: A 2 dm³ flask of a gas at 3 atm is connected to a 4 dm³ flask of the same gas at 1.5 atm. The temperature stays constant. The final pressure is:
x: Total PV = (3 × 2) + (1.5 × 4) = 12 dm³ atm, shared over 6 dm³, so P = 12/6 = 2 atm. Simply averaging the two pressures gives the wrong 2.25 atm.

q: A balloon holds 2.00 dm³ of air at 0 °C. It is warmed to 100 °C at constant pressure. Its new volume is about:
x: V₂ = V₁ × T₂/T₁ = 2.00 × 373/273 ≈ 2.73 dm³. The 1.46 dm³ value comes from inverting the temperature ratio.

q: In calculations using Charles's law, temperatures must be in kelvin because:
o: The kelvin scale gives larger numbers that are easier to divide
Volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature, not to Celsius temperature
Gas volume does not change with temperature in °C
Celsius temperatures can only be used for liquids
x: V ∝ T holds only when T is measured from absolute zero. On the Celsius scale, 0 °C does not mean zero volume, so ratios of Celsius temperatures give wrong answers.

q: A partly blown-up balloon is put in a freezer and it shrinks. According to the kinetic theory, this is because the gas molecules:
o: Become larger and stick to the balloon wall
Escape through the rubber in the cold
Slow down, so at the same outside pressure the gas takes up less space
x: Cooling lowers the average speed of the molecules, so they push on the balloon wall less. The balloon shrinks until the inside pressure again matches the outside pressure.

q: Graphs of volume against absolute temperature are drawn for the same gas sample at two pressures, P₁ and P₂, where P₁ is higher than P₂. Which line is steeper?
o: The line at the lower pressure P₂
The line at the higher pressure P₁
Both lines have the same slope
Neither, because both graphs are curves
x: At constant pressure V = (nR/P)T, so the slope nR/P is larger when P is smaller. Both graphs are straight lines through the origin.

q: A gas is heated at constant pressure from 200 K to 300 K. Its volume increases by:
x: V₂/V₁ = 300/200 = 1.5, so the volume rises by 50%. The 33% answer comes from dividing the change by the final temperature instead of the starting one.

q: The absolute temperature of a fixed mass of gas is doubled at constant pressure. Its density:
x: By Charles's law the volume doubles. The mass stays the same, so density (mass/volume) halves.

q: Charles's law applies when the amount of gas and which other quantity are kept constant?
x: Charles's law relates volume and temperature for a fixed amount of gas at constant pressure. Density changes as the volume changes.

q: A temperature of 400 K on the Celsius scale is:
x: °C = K − 273, so 400 − 273 = 127 °C. Adding 273 instead gives the wrong 673 °C.

q: Which statement about absolute zero is correct?
o: It is easily reached by cooling helium gas
It is the temperature at which water freezes
It has never been reached, although temperatures very close to it have been achieved
It is the lowest temperature only for ideal gases, not for other substances
x: Absolute zero (0 K) is the lowest possible temperature for all matter. It has never actually been reached, though scientists have come within a tiny fraction of a kelvin.

q: A gas is at 0 °C. To what Celsius temperature must it be heated to double its absolute temperature?
x: 0 °C is 273 K; doubling gives 546 K, which is 546 − 273 = 273 °C. The 546 °C answer forgets to convert back to Celsius.

q: Which of the following temperatures is NOT possible?
x: Nothing can be colder than absolute zero, about −273 °C. −300 °C lies below it, so it is impossible; −270 °C is about 3 K.

q: A gas occupies 300 cm³ at 27 °C. At constant pressure, at what temperature would its volume theoretically be 100 cm³?
x: Volume is proportional to absolute temperature: 27 °C = 300 K, and one-third of that is 100 K, which is −173 °C. Dividing 27 °C by 3 gives the wrong 9 °C.

q: Gas X is at 0 °C and gas Y is at 273 °C. Compared with the molecules of X, the molecules of Y have an average kinetic energy that is:
x: Kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature: 273 K for X and 546 K for Y, a ratio of 1 : 2. The Celsius values cannot be used for this ratio.

q: At 1 atm, water freezes at 273 K. On the kelvin scale, it boils at:
x: Water boils at 100 °C, and 100 + 273 = 373 K. A change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K.

q: The ideal gas equation PV = nRT becomes Boyle's law when:
o: n and P are kept constant
P and T are kept constant
n and T are kept constant
n and V are kept constant
x: With n and T fixed, nRT is a constant, so PV = constant, which is Boyle's law. Constant n and P gives Charles's law instead.

q: For a fixed amount of gas kept at constant volume, the ideal gas equation shows that:
x: From PV = nRT, P/T = nR/V. With n and V fixed, P/T is constant, so pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

q: A sealed 8.21 dm³ cylinder at 400 K holds a gas at a pressure of 2 atm. Taking R as 0.0821 in these units, how much gas does it contain, in moles?
4.4 g of a gas occupies 1.12 dm³ at 2 atm and 273 K. What is its molar mass? (R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; 0.0821 × 273 ≈ 22.4)
x: M = mRT/PV = (4.4 × 22.4)/(2 × 1.12) = 98.56/2.24 = 44 g mol⁻¹. Leaving out the pressure gives the wrong 88.

q: What is the density of oxygen gas, O₂, at 2 atm and 273 K? (O = 16; 0.0821 × 273 ≈ 22.4)
x: d = PM/RT = (2 × 32)/22.4 ≈ 2.86 g dm⁻³. Forgetting the pressure of 2 atm gives 1.43, the density at STP.

q: The pressure on a fixed amount of an ideal gas is halved while its absolute temperature is doubled. Its volume becomes:
x: V = nRT/P. Doubling T doubles V and halving P doubles it again, so the volume becomes four times larger.

q: Which of the following is NOT a correct form of the ideal gas equation? (m = mass, M = molar mass, d = density)
x: Volume increases with temperature, so T must be in the numerator: PV = nRT. Putting n = m/M gives PV = (m/M)RT, and using d = m/V gives PM = dRT.

q: At the same temperature and pressure, 2 dm³ of H₂ and 2 dm³ of CO₂ are taken. The ratio of the mass of H₂ to the mass of CO₂ is: (H 1, C 12, O 16)
x: Equal volumes at the same T and P contain equal numbers of moles, so the mass ratio equals the molar mass ratio: 2 : 44 = 1 : 22.

q: The gas constant R has the value 8.314 when it is expressed in:
x: 1 joule = 1 newton metre, so 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ is the same as 8.314 N m K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. In the other units R is 0.0821, 1.987 and 82.1.

q: Using SI values for 1 mol of an ideal gas, P = 101325 N m⁻², V = 0.022414 m³ and T = 273.15 K, the value of R obtained is:
x: R = (101325 × 0.022414)/(1 × 273.15) ≈ 8.314 N m K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. This is the SI value, because SI units of pressure and volume were used.

q: The unit dm³ atm, used in one value of R, is a unit of:
x: Pressure × volume = (force/area) × volume = force × distance, which is work or energy. This is why R can be given both in dm³ atm and in joules.

q: Which pair gives two values of R that are BOTH correct?
o: 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
8.314 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and 0.0821 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and 1.987 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
62.4 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
x: R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. The value 1.987 is in calories, and 62.4 is in dm³ mm Hg.

q: Using R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, one dm³ atm is equal to about:
x: 8.314/0.0821 ≈ 101.3, so 1 dm³ atm ≈ 101.3 J. Dividing the other way round gives the wrong 0.0099 J.

q: For 1 mol of an ideal gas at 273 K, the product PV is about: (R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
x: PV = nRT = 1 × 0.0821 × 273 ≈ 22.4 dm³ atm. This is why 1 mol occupies 22.4 dm³ at 1 atm and 273 K.

q: When the units are kept the same, the value of R:
o: Does not depend on the amount, temperature or pressure of the gas
x: R is a universal constant: in fixed units it has one value for all ideal gases under all conditions. Only a change of units changes its number.

q: An ideal gas could never be liquefied, however much it was cooled or compressed, because:
o: Its molecules occupy the whole container volume
Its molecules have no attractive forces between them
x: Liquefaction needs attractive forces to hold molecules together. The ideal gas model assumes none, so only real gases, which do attract, can be liquefied.

q: The excluded-volume constant b of a real gas is measured in:
x: b is the excluded volume per mole, so it is measured in dm³ mol⁻¹. The units atm dm⁶ mol⁻² belong to the constant a.

q: Which gas has the smallest van der Waals constant a?
x: a measures the attractive forces between molecules. Helium atoms are small, non-polar and hard to polarise, so their attractions are the weakest; NH₃, with hydrogen bonding, has a large a.

q: A real gas at moderate pressure has a compressibility factor Z = PV/nRT less than 1. This shows that:
o: The volume of the molecules dominates, so the gas is less compressible than an ideal gas
Attractive forces dominate, so the gas is more compressible than an ideal gas
The gas is behaving exactly as an ideal gas
The molecules have no kinetic energy
x: Attractions pull molecules together, so the measured PV is smaller than nRT and Z is below 1. When molecular volume dominates, as at very high pressure, Z rises above 1.

q: In the van der Waals equation, the term added to the measured pressure P to correct for intermolecular attractions is:
x: The equation is (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT. The term an²/V² corrects pressure for attractions, and nb corrects volume for the size of the molecules.

q: For real gases, which assumption of the kinetic theory remains valid?
o: The molecules themselves have negligible volume
Molecules are in continuous random motion
There are no attractive forces between molecules
The whole container volume is free for molecular motion
x: Real gas molecules are still in constant random motion. The faulty postulates are those about negligible molecular volume and no attractions, which is why the free volume is less than the container volume.

q: In the van der Waals equation, both correction terms, an²/V² and nb, become negligible when the gas:
o: Is highly compressed at low temperature
Occupies a very large volume, at low pressure
Is cooled close to its boiling point
x: In a very large volume, an²/V² is tiny and nb is small compared with V, so the equation reduces to PV = nRT. This is why real gases are nearly ideal at low pressure.

q: A gas that would obey PV = nRT exactly at every temperature and pressure is called:
x: An ideal gas obeys the gas laws exactly under all conditions. Real gases, including the noble gases, only approach this at low pressure and high temperature.
